sections.content: Time to talk about yourself! In Spanish, there are two ways to say 'I am' — 'soy' and 'estoy.' They aren't interchangeable. Soy is for permanent things (who you are), and estoy is for temporary things (how you feel right now). This lesson gives you the power to introduce yourself beyond just your name.

Use 'estoy' for temporary states like feelings and location

items.notes: Temporary state — how you feel now

sections.heading: Ser vs. Estar — The Two 'To Be' Verbs
sections.content: Spanish has two verbs for 'to be': SER and ESTAR. Think of it this way: SER = who you are (identity, origin, profession, nationality, personality). ESTAR = how you are or where you are (feelings, mood, location, temporary conditions). 'Soy' is the 'I' form of ser. 'Estoy' is the 'I' form of estar. Examples: 'Soy americano' (I am American — that won't change). 'Estoy cansado' (I am tired — that will change). A quick trick: if the condition can change by tomorrow, use ESTAR. If it defines who you are, use SER.

sections.content: Want to tell people what you enjoy? In Spanish, you don't say 'I like coffee' — you say 'Coffee is pleasing to me.' It sounds weird in English, but once you get the pattern, it's easy. This lesson covers me gusta, food, activities, and how to ask others what they like.

sections.heading: The Gustar Pattern
sections.content: Gustar doesn't work like English 'to like.' In Spanish, the thing you like is the subject. Think of it as: 'To me, coffee is pleasing' = Me gusta el café. The verb agrees with the THING, not with you. One thing = gusta. Multiple things = gustan. Me gusta el café (one thing — coffee). Me gustan los tacos (multiple things — tacos). To say you don't like something, just put 'no' before 'me': No me gusta el frío (I don't like the cold). To ask someone: ¿Te gusta? (informal) or ¿Le gusta? (formal). You will almost always only need 'gusta' and 'gustan' — just two forms to remember!

Even a simple '¿Le gusta el café?' while they're at the coffee station builds connection.

sections.content: Family is one of the most common conversation topics. Whether a coworker shares photos of their kids or a customer mentions they're shopping for their family, knowing this vocabulary lets you connect on a personal level. Let's learn to talk about the people who matter most.

sections.heading: Possessives and Tengo
sections.content: To say 'my' in Spanish: 'mi' for one thing, 'mis' for multiple. Mi hermano (my brother), mis hermanos (my brothers). To talk about how many family members you have, use 'tengo' (I have): Tengo tres hermanos = I have three brothers. Tengo una hija = I have one daughter. No tengo hijos = I don't have kids. Note: In Spanish, when referring to mixed-gender groups, the masculine plural is used. 'Mis hermanos' can mean 'my brothers' or 'my siblings' (brothers and sisters together). Same with 'mis hijos' — it can mean 'my sons' or 'my children.'

sections.heading: Talking About What You Do
sections.content: To describe your job, you have several patterns. For your role: Soy + job title (no article needed!). 'Soy cajero' NOT 'Soy un cajero.' For where you work: Trabajo en + place. 'Trabajo en Kwik Trip.' For your schedule: Trabajo de + day + a + day. 'Trabajo de lunes a viernes.' For your hours: Trabajo hasta las + time. 'Trabajo hasta las diez.' To talk about what you do: Yo + verb. 'Yo ayudo a los clientes' (I help the customers). 'Yo limpio la tienda' (I clean the store). Notice how simple it is — subject + verb + the rest.

sections.heading: Level 1 Grammar Review
sections.content: Here are the key grammar points from Level 1: (1) Formal vs. Informal: Use usted with customers and strangers; tú with friends and peers. (2) Ser vs. Estar: Ser (soy) for permanent things — identity, origin, profession. Estar (estoy) for temporary things — feelings, location, current state. (3) Gustar pattern: Me gusta + singular thing. Me gustan + plural things. The thing you like is the subject, not you. (4) Tengo: I have. Used for family, possessions, and age (Tengo 25 años). (5) Gender: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine, -a are feminine. Adjectives match: cansado/cansada, americano/americana. (6) Plurals: Add -s to vowels, -es to consonants. Mi becomes mis.
